qs.q: What is the primary hemodynamic consequence that leads to Eisenmenger syndrome in an uncorrected left-to-right shunt?
qs.e: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when a long-standing left-to-right shunt causes irreversible pulmonary hypertension, eventually reversing the shunt to a right-to-left direction. Left ventricular volume overload precedes this but is not the defining final pathophysiology.

qs.q: A 3-year-old child with a large, unrepaired ventricular septal defect develops Eisenmenger's syndrome. What primary physiological alteration characterizes this complication?
o: Spontaneous closure of the septal defect with resolution of heart failure
Marked reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance elevating the Qp:Qs ratio
Severe systemic hypotension driven by excessive peripheral afterload drop
Reversal of the shunt to right-to-left causing progressive central cyanosis
qs.e: Eisenmenger's syndrome occurs when chronic left-to-right shunting causes severe pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension, eventually reversing the shunt to right-to-left. This process involves irreversible pulmonary vascular remodeling rather than a drop in resistance or spontaneous defect closure.

qs.q: Surgical closure of a complete ventricular septal defect is usually performed before what age to prevent Eisenmenger syndrome?
qs.e: Early repair (<6 months) avoids the development of Eisenmenger. Delaying beyond 1 year increases the risk.

qs.q: Which clinical sign suggests that a patient with a previously known left-to-right shunt has developed Eisenmenger's syndrome?
o: Onset of severe diaphoresis and poor feeding during infancy
Worsening of the continuous machinery murmur and massive hepatomegaly
Development of a loud holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border
Appearance of cyanosis and clubbing with disappearance of heart failure symptoms
qs.e: In Eisenmenger's syndrome, the pulmonary vascular resistance increases until the shunt reverses (right-to-left), leading to cyanosis, clubbing, and the disappearance of heart failure symptoms and murmurs. Active heart failure signs instead characterize the pre-Eisenmenger phase.

o: The tricuspid valve is completely absent
qs.e: Eisenmenger syndrome is characterized by the reversal of a left-to-right shunt to a right-to-left shunt, caused by severe pulmonary hypertension.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Eisenmenger syndrome is the irreversible reversal of a long‑standing left‑to‑right shunt to right‑to‑left due to pulmonary hypertension, producing cyanosis and right‑heart failure.

sections.p: A chronic left‑to‑right shunt (often VSD, ASD, PDA) that, after years of pulmonary overcirculation, leads to pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal. Diagnosis requires evidence of cyanosis, right‑heart strain, and a reversed shunt on imaging.
b: Reversed shunt on cardiac MRI or echo

sections.p: Staging follows WHO functional class and pulmonary pressure ranges, guiding prognosis and transplant candidacy.
Congenital defects that create a large left‑to‑right shunt are the primary culprits. In low‑resource settings, infections and conditions that raise pulmonary pressures can accelerate progression.
Patients develop progressive cyanosis, clubbing, exertional dyspnea, and right‑heart failure symptoms. Early signs may be subtle and mimic other conditions.
Key tests confirm shunt reversal, quantify pulmonary pressures, and assess right‑heart function. When resources are limited, clinical signs and basic imaging guide management.
Acute right‑heart failure, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and sudden death are life‑threatening complications.

Treat the underlying cause if possible, provide supportive care, and prepare for lung transplantation when indicated. Pharmacologic choices aim to lower pulmonary pressures without worsening right‑heart failure.
Regular monitoring of oxygen saturation, right‑heart function, and pulmonary pressures is essential. Prevention focuses on early detection and repair of congenital shunts.
b: Referral for surgical repair before pulmonary hypertension develops

sections.p: Other cyanotic heart diseases and pulmonary hypertension causes can mimic Eisenmenger.
Normal chest X-ray or mild echo findings may mask severe pulmonary hypertension; low SpO2 can be misinterpreted as lung disease.
b: Normal pulmonary artery size on X-ray despite high pressures
